scope: Chicago lakefront from Ardmore Avenue to 71st Street, north-up aerial reference for illustrated map correction

sources.note: Preferred built-feature reference. Item title says 2025 while description says flown in 2026; exact acquisition year was not resolved. White areas offshore are imagery coverage gaps, not land. Leaf-off imagery makes roads and lawns clear.
2019 NAIP leaf-on imagery. Good for distinguishing tree canopy from lawn. Downtown catalog acquisition date is 2019-08-02. This is a baseline, not current conditions.

panels.name: 01-edgewater-uptown
findings: Dense rectilinear city blocks immediately west of the lakefront park and Lake Shore Drive.
Ardmore/Osterman is a beach and narrow lawn strip, backed by high-rises; no broad woodland.
Foster Beach is a small sandy scallop north of the wide Montrose peninsula.
Montrose peninsula contains open recreation fields, a running track, beach, roads and parking. Its more concentrated canopy is at Montrose Point / bird sanctuary on the southeast tip.
Montrose Harbor lies south of the beach, has its own distinctive crescent basin and dock pattern.

panels.name: 02-lincoln-park-gold-coast
findings: Lakeview and Lincoln Park neighborhoods are a dense street/building grid west of the park boundary.
Belmont and Diversey harbors are distinct elongated basins; their shapes should come from geometry rather than repeated pictorial harbor stamps.
Lincoln Park contains open sports fields, ponds and lagoons, zoo structures, formal grounds, lawns and scattered groves. Canopy is not a continuous belt.
North Avenue Beach is a large crescent with long sandy shore; nearby fields and parking are open.
South of North Avenue to Oak Street, Gold Coast buildings approach Lake Shore Drive directly. Do not paint a forest over these blocks.

panels.name: 03-downtown-museum-campus
findings: Streeterville is dense city blocks with high-rise buildings, Chicago River flowing west-east, and only small landscaped patches.
Navy Pier projects due east. Its long rectangular roof/boardwalk is south of the separate broad rectangular water-filtration-plant peninsula.
Ohio Street Beach lies west/northwest of Navy Pier, near its landward root.
Grant Park is a formal rectangle of lawns, promenades, fields and tree rows; Buckingham Fountain is a circular landmark within open formal grounds.
Museum Campus has distinct buildings separated by lawns/plazas: Field Museum western/southern block, Shedd north/east of Field, Adler at the eastern tip along Solidarity Drive.
Soldier Field is south of Field Museum. Burnham Harbor is east of Soldier Field and west of Northerly Island.

panels.name: 04-burnham-hyde-park
findings: McCormick Place is a very large built complex, visibly unlike a park or grove.
31st Street Harbor is a large oval/crescent man-made harbor south of its beach.
Most Burnham lakefront is an open grass ribbon with sparse trees between shoreline and the road/rail corridor.
Bronzeville and Kenwood show residential street blocks west of the highway/rail corridor.
Hyde Park has dense city fabric and waterfront apartment towers. Promontory Point is a recognizable eastward peninsula with open central lawn and trees near the perimeter.

panels.name: 05-jackson-south-shore
findings: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is a large building at the north of Jackson Park with formal open grounds.
Wooded Island and lagoon margins carry concentrated canopy. Large golf and recreation areas to the south are open lawn with tree rows.
63rd Street Beach and its small beach house are east of Lake Shore Drive. The building should not obscure the beach's true extent.
Jackson Park inner and outer harbors have separate identifiable basins and are not interchangeable with the northern harbor illustrations.
South Shore Cultural Center is a small estate/campus within a coastal lawn and golf landscape; neighborhood city blocks lie immediately west.
Recent construction footprint west of the Jackson Park lagoons differs from the older 2019 survey; use current map geometry and recent Cook imagery here.

rendering_corrections: Remove random forest stamps distributed continuously by shoreline Y; place canopy only in real known green areas, retaining lawns, sports fields, sand and pavement.
Preserve enough city width west of the shoreline to show dense buildings, streets, rail and Lake Shore Drive; avoid the left-edge washout erasing the urban landscape.

Anchor each attraction at its exact coordinate with a small marker and optionally a thin leader to its illustration; scale pictorial art so it does not conceal adjacent attractions or imply a kilometer-wide building.
Use actual harbor and pier geometry as the main depiction, not repeated generic harbor pictures.
Place Lake Michigan text east of the local shoreline at the label's Y, not at a fixed global X; include text width in the offshore clearance check.
North is up and east/lake is right; the shoreline's longitude changes substantially down the route, so camera and label placement must follow it.
comparison_of_surveys: The major shoreline, beach, harbor, street-grid and landmark relationships are consistent between the 2019 USGS and newer Cook County panels.

The newer Cook County panel shows a major construction footprint west of the Jackson Park lagoons, replacing open grounds visible in 2019. Do not recreate the older lawn footprint as a current feature.

The newer Cook County survey is substantially leaf-off. Reduced visible canopy relative to the summer 2019 survey should not be interpreted as tree removal. Use 2019 leaf-on imagery for canopy/lawn distinction and newer imagery for built footprints.
Beach width and exposed sand differ between surveys; preserve mapped current shoreline geometry rather than tracing transient waterline color from a single aerial date.
White rectangles over Lake Michigan in Cook imagery and black offshore gaps in portions of USGS imagery indicate no-data coverage gaps, not geography.
